compute.anchor_note: Compute density per mm2 is derived from one published GPU's dense tensor roofs divided by its published whole-die area, then scaled by the node logic-density ratio. Applying a whole-die-derived density to a modelled design's COMPUTE-ONLY area is the model's stated compute assumption: it is conservative in that an A100 die spends area on HBM PHY, L2 and schedulers that the density is nevertheless charged for, and optimistic in that NVIDIA's tensor cores are a highly tuned datapath. Newer parts are denser: B200 achieves 2.81e12 FP8 ops/s/mm2 at 4NP against 1.50e12 predicted by scaling A100 INT8, so this anchor understates a 2026 design by roughly 1.9x.

bf16.note: A100 80GB SXM, 312 TFLOPS dense BF16 tensor (624 with structured sparsity, not used)

fp4.note: A100 publishes 1248 TOPS dense INT4; FP4 e2m1 is taken as the same datapath area as INT4

fp8.note: A100 publishes 624 TOPS dense INT8. An FP8 e4m3 multiply-accumulate is taken as the same datapath area as INT8; A100 itself has no FP8 unit, so this is a density transfer, not a claim about Ampere.

w4a8_density_rule.note: A 4-bit-weight by 8-bit-activation multiply-accumulate is bounded below by the w8a8 datapath (no narrowing credit taken) and above by the w4a4 datapath. NVIDIA publishes both endpoints on one die, so the bracket is published and only the interpolation is a judgement. Both endpoints are also reported so the bracket, not the midpoint, is what the reader checks.

compute.note: fraction of the peak tensor roof a real decode kernel sustains, covering pipeline bubbles, tail effects and non-tensor interleave
compute.source: carried over from src/opentallas/schema.py ArchitectureProfile default

expert_router_imbalance.note: Multiplier on the per-region sweep depth, applied ON TOP OF the expected busiest-region load rather than instead of it. This replaces efficiencies.expert_load_balance = 0.85, which was documented as carrying 'the sweep depth is set by the busiest region rather than the mean' while the code divided the MEAN engaged-region load by it. The busiest region is now computed explicitly (roofline.expected_max_region_load), and a single constant cannot stand in for it: the ratio of the busiest region to the mean runs from 1.0 at batch 1 to about 3.0 at batch 64. What is left for this parameter is the residual imbalance of a TRAINED router against the uniform-random draw the busiest-region statistic assumes. It is 1.0 -- the neutral value, which makes it inert -- because no trace exists to set it, and because a parameter must not take its value from the answer it is wanted to produce. The per-region sweep depth is exactly linear in it, so a trace showing a 1.3x hot-expert bias moves every per-region number by 1.3x.
expert_router_imbalance.source: no measured routing trace for a per-region compute-in-ROM fabric

hbm_bandwidth.note: applied to both weight and KV traffic on an HBM device
hbm_bandwidth.source: commonly measured STREAM-class fraction of HBM peak on datacentre GPUs

hbm_capacity.note: fraction of physical HBM available to checkpoint and KV after runtime workspace, allocator and safety reserve
hbm_capacity.source: carried over from src/opentallas/schema.py ArchitectureProfile default

no_clock_derate_rationale.note: No separate clock-efficiency derate is applied anywhere in this model. A100's 312 TFLOPS, WSE-2's 20 PB/s and the HBM bandwidths are achieved rates at shipping clocks, not timing-signoff targets, so charging a further clock derate on top would double-count. The only derates applied are the sustained-fraction ones named above.
no_clock_derate_rationale.source: every density in this table is derived from an ACHIEVED shipping-silicon figure

rom_read_bandwidth.note: Fraction of the ROM array's peak sweep rate sustained in practice. A mask-ROM sweep is the most regular access pattern available -- a compile-time-fixed linear walk of the whole array with no arbitration, no conflicts and no refresh -- so 0.75 is a conservative charge and 0.90-1.00 is arguable. The study reports the underated ceiling alongside it because this derate moves the ROM answer directly.

sram_read_bandwidth.note: fraction of the SRAM array's peak read rate sustained by a real gather pattern

stage_balance.note: penalty applied to a multi-device pipeline for imperfect layer balance across devices
stage_balance.source: no measured layer-to-device partition for the modelled designs

hbm_j_per_byte.note: 3.9 pJ/bit for HBM2 access energy, converted to 31.2 pJ/byte. Cross-check: A100 at its full 2039 GB/s implies 63.6 W of HBM access power, consistent with published board-level HBM power.
hbm_j_per_byte.source: O'Connor et al., Fine-Grained DRAM, MICRO 2017

grade_definitions.assumed: no published value found; a stated judgement that must be swept
grade_definitions.derived: computed from published/measured entries by a formula stated in the note
grade_definitions.executed: obtained by running something in this repository -- the reference oracle, a deployment, a campaign -- with the artifact holding the numbers committed and named in the entry's `artifact` field. Distinct from `measured`, which means fabricated silicon in a peer-reviewed venue; almost nothing this program does is that, and its absence was pushing executed values into grades that fitted them worse.

max_beachfront_utilization.note: A100 80GB places five HBM2e stacks on an 826 mm2 die: 5 x 12 mm of pitch against a 115 mm perimeter, or 52%. Shipping parts therefore use roughly 50-60% of the die edge for HBM, the rest going to host, scale-up and power. 0.60 is taken as the ceiling, which makes a modelled ROM part's HBM beachfront no more aggressive than NVIDIA's own. This matters: at equal die area both sides then have the SAME KV bandwidth ceiling, and the ROM part's advantage is only that it does not also spend that bandwidth on weights.

phy_area_mm2_per_stack.note: A 1024-bit HBM PHY plus controller is commonly quoted between 8 and 15 mm2 at 7 nm class. Sweep that range.
phy_area_mm2_per_stack.source: no vendor-published HBM PHY macro area

stack_beachfront_mm.note: 11 mm HBM package edge plus routing keep-out; carried over from configs/hardware/technology_inputs.json

stack_capacity_bytes.note: A100 80GB carries five active HBM2e stacks; 80 GB / 5

max_beachfront_utilization.note: B200 places eight HBM3E stacks on a ~1600 mm2 package: 8 x 12 mm against a 160 mm perimeter, or 60%. Shipping parts therefore use roughly 50-60% of the die edge for HBM, the rest going to host, scale-up and power. 0.60 is taken as the ceiling, which makes a modelled ROM part's HBM beachfront no more aggressive than NVIDIA's own. This matters: at equal die area both sides then have the SAME KV bandwidth ceiling, and the ROM part's advantage is only that it does not also spend that bandwidth on weights.

phy_area_mm2_per_stack.source: no vendor-published HBM PHY macro area

published_stack_ceiling.note: Micron HBM3E: over 1.2 TB/s per stack, 24 GB at 8-high and 36 GB at 12-high. Retained as the upper cross-check on the shipping-system-derived values above; not used by the model.

stack_bandwidth_bytes_s.note: B200 SXM delivers 8 TB/s across eight HBM3E stacks: 8 TB/s / 8. Micron publishes over 1.2 TB/s per HBM3E stack at full pin speed (https://www.micron.com/products/memory/hbm/hbm3e), so 1.0 TB/s is the rate a shipping system actually clocks and is the conservative choice.

stack_beachfront_mm.note: 11 mm x 11 mm HBM3E package plus routing keep-out

stack_capacity_bytes.note: B200 SXM ships 180 GB across eight HBM3E stacks: 180 GB / 8. Micron's published HBM3E 12-high part is 36 GB per stack (https://www.micron.com/about/blog/applications/ai/micron-continues-memory-industry-leadership-with-hbm3e-12-high-36gb), so this is the SHIPPING-SYSTEM figure rather than the densest available die stack. Deriving it from the reference GPU keeps both sides of the iso-area comparison on identical memory technology, which is the point.

hbm.note: An HBM3 channel is split into two 32-bit pseudo-channels and the minimum burst is 8, so the smallest read that reaches the die is 32 bytes. A 68-byte index entry therefore costs 96 bytes. Graded assumed rather than published because the number is reconstructed from the interface geometry rather than read off a datasheet line.
hbm.source: HBM3/3E pseudo-channel width times burst length; no vendor erratum consulted for this program

sram.note: The row width a wide on-die SRAM macro delivers per access. 128 bytes is a common leading-node macro word for a bandwidth-optimised array; a narrower 64-byte macro halves the waste on a 68-byte entry only because 68 still spills into a second word. Sweep 64 to 256.
sram.source: no vendor macro datasheet for the target on-die arrays

index_layout.note: Where a compressed-sparse layer's 68-byte index entry sits relative to the 583-byte payload entry it describes. 'interleaved' is the natural result of writing both at generation time and makes every index entry its own access; 'contiguous' packs the index array separately so the scan is one sequential run and granule rounding costs nothing. The two differ by more than 1.6x on DeepSeek-V4-Flash at 200K context, where 72% of the KV read is that scan. Stated as a named choice because a design can simply choose the cheap one -- and because a model that silently assumed the cheap one would be claiming a design decision as a fact.
index_layout.source: layout CHOICE, not a physical constant; no released serving implementation inspected for this program

kv.purpose: How KV bytes are actually moved, as opposed to how many the algorithm needs. workload.kv_traffic counts algorithmic bytes; a memory system moves whole granules, and for a sparse-index model most of the KV read is a scan of entries far smaller than one granule.

array_pass_boundaries_per_layer.note: Serially dependent matrix passes in one decoder layer. Four is the standard block; a fused QKV gives three and a separate router pass gives five. Graded assumed rather than derived because the model profiles do not state a pass structure -- operations.operation_inventory counts arithmetic, not passes.
array_pass_boundaries_per_layer.source: transformer block structure: QKV, attention output, gate/up, down

global_wire_delay_s_per_mm.note: 100-250 ps/mm is the commonly quoted range for an optimally repeatered global interconnect at 7 nm class; it is flat with scaling because repeater insertion linearises RC. The traversal DISTANCE is derived from the floorplan rather than assumed: sqrt(reticle.area_mm2), which is one die edge, taken as the mean distance an activation broadcast covers. Charged once per array-pass boundary and once for the KV round trip.
global_wire_delay_s_per_mm.source: repeatered global-wire delay per millimetre at a leading node

layer_barrier_s.note: A layer transition is a barrier: every lane's partial result must be retired and the residual formed before the next layer's activation exists. On a distributed fabric this is a reduction plus a broadcast of the completion signal, on top of the wire delay charged separately. Charged once per layer.
layer_barrier_s.source: no published synchronisation cost for this class of part

pipeline_fill_drain_s.note: Fill and drain across the boundary between two SERIALLY DEPENDENT array passes. The second pass cannot begin until the first has retired, so the boundary costs a full traversal of the pipeline. 32 ns is roughly 32 stages at a 1 GHz fabric clock; the low end is a shallow accumulator tree over 4k lanes (12-16 levels) and the high end is a systolic drain of a 128-deep array. Charged once per array-pass boundary. THIS IS THE LARGEST TERM IN THE BLOCK and the widest band; the anchor is reported at both ends of it.
pipeline_fill_drain_s.source: no published array pipeline depth for this class of part

latency.purpose: The serial per-layer cost that no amount of bandwidth removes. Before this block the only latency in the model was links.*.hop_latency_s, charged at inter-partition boundaries, so a single_chip design had a decode step with no fixed cost at all. EVERY TERM HERE IS DERIVED FROM A PRIMITIVE THAT EXISTS INDEPENDENTLY OF THE TAALAS HC1 ANCHOR, and each carries range_low/range_high. The anchor gate is evaluated at both ends of that band and reports where it lands as an OUTCOME. No term is chosen to close the anchor gap: doing that would turn a validation gate into a one-parameter curve fit, and the gate is load-bearing (checklist W12.5). Charged per layer: sequencer_issue_decode + layer_barrier + one KV round trip (sram_access + one global traversal) + array_pass_boundaries_per_layer x (pipeline_fill_drain + one global traversal). Compressed-sparse layers additionally pay sparse_index_dependency.

sequencer_issue_decode_s.note: Instruction fetch, decode and operand setup for one layer's command stream in a statically scheduled sequencer. A few cycles at a ~1 GHz fabric clock; 1-8 ns spans a single-cycle issue to a deeply decoded microcoded one. Charged once per layer.
sequencer_issue_decode_s.source: no published sequencer for a mask-ROM or compute-in-ROM inference die

sparse_index_dependency_s.note: Charged only on layers whose profile says compressed_sparse. The gather address is not known until the index scan's top-k has completed, so the layer pays a selection over tens of thousands of candidates followed by a round trip that cannot be prefetched. 128 ns sits above an SRAM round trip and below a DRAM row cycle, which is the bracket a top-k-then-gather falls in. The bytes of the scan itself are charged against bandwidth, with their access granularity, in the kv block.
sparse_index_dependency_s.source: no published top-k selection pipeline at this candidate count

sram_access_s.note: Access time of a large on-die SRAM macro: address decode, wordline rise, bitline develop, sense and output latch. 1-4 ns brackets the published range for bandwidth-optimised leading-node macros of the size this model places. Charged once per layer, as the read half of the KV round trip; the KV BYTES are charged separately against bandwidth and this is only the dependency bandwidth cannot overlap.
sram_access_s.source: no vendor macro datasheet for the target on-die arrays

fabric.note: scale-out Ethernet is a switched fat tree

hop_latency_s.note: InfiniBand/Ethernet class scale-out hop. Not measured.

bytes_s.note: DGX A100 carries eight single-port ConnectX-6 HDR adapters at 200 Gb/s for eight GPUs -- "a one-to-one relationship between the IO cards and the GPUs" -- so 200 Gb/s = 25 GB/s of payload per GPU in one direction. That is one twelfth of the NVLink 3 rate beside it, which is the whole reason the domain boundary has to be modelled. Achievable RDMA payload is 88-98% of line rate, or 22.0-24.6 GB/s; the line rate is used, which favours the GPU.
bytes_s.source: NVIDIA DGX A100 System Architecture WP-10083-001_v01 (July 2020)

domain_size.note: NVIDIA Quantum QM8700: 40 HDR 200 Gb/s ports per switch

fabric.note: scale-out InfiniBand is a switched fat tree, so a collective spanning more endpoints than one tier reaches has to climb tiers

hop_latency_s.note: GPU-buffer to GPU-buffer inter-node latency, which is what a decode step actually pays -- not the 1.07 us CPU-memory MPI ping-pong, which is the figure usually quoted and is not reachable from a GPU. De Sensi et al. (SC24) measured 3.7-5.7 us across five production supercomputers, and on Leonardo (A100 + HDR InfiniBand) 4.33 us within one switch rising to 5.56 us across switches. The switch silicon is a small part of it: an NVIDIA Quantum HDR switch is published at sub-130 ns port to port and a ConnectX-6 adapter at sub-600 ns, so the remainder is adapter, protocol and software. Stated at 4.5 us and swept 3.7-5.7 us.
hop_latency_s.source: De Sensi et al., Exploring GPU-to-GPU Communication: Insights into Supercomputer Interconnects, SC24, arXiv:2408.14090 ; https://network.nvidia.com/files/doc-2020/pb-qm8700.pdf

bytes_s.note: DGX B200 carries eight ConnectX-7 single-port cards for eight GPUs at up to 400 Gb/s InfiniBand, so 400 Gb/s = 50 GB/s of payload per GPU in one direction. Cross-checks against the HGX B200 networking row of 0.8 TB/s = 8 x 400 Gb/s x 2 directions. Achievable RDMA payload is 44-48 GB/s; the line rate is used, which favours the GPU.

domain_size.source: Cerebras CS Weight Streaming white paper, section 6.4 (SwarmX)

fabric.note: SwarmX is a broadcast-reduce tree; a rack of wafers is modelled as one switched domain, which is the optimistic reading
fabric.source: Cerebras CS Weight Streaming white paper, section 6.4 (SwarmX)

hop_latency_s.note: Cerebras publishes no SwarmX latency figure in any form. SwarmX is a broadcast-reduce tree over 100 GbE, so the class of the link is known even where the number is not: 100 GbE RDMA between accelerator buffers is the same 3.7-5.7 us class the InfiniBand measurements give, and 5.0 us is taken as the point. The low end of the sweep, 1.0 us, is a purpose-built wafer-to-wafer link better than anything shipping; the high end, 10.0 us, is a tree with a second level. This is the number that decides whether a twelve-wafer machine is one machine or twelve, and this study previously charged it the on-wafer stitched-mesh hop of 100 ns -- the ROM-side mirror of charging a GPU cluster a 672-way pipeline.

hop_latency_s.note: NVLink point-to-point sits around 1 us for small messages. A real all-reduce is two phases through a switch plus launch and synchronisation overhead, so 1.5 us is optimistic; 3-10 us is common in practice. Sweep upward, never downward.

bytes_s.note: A100 SXM NVLink 3.0: twelve links at 25 GB/s per direction each, published as 600 GB/s bidirectional per GPU, so 300 GB/s of payload in one direction. The n6_vs_a100 study charges this fabric to BOTH sides -- the ROM array and the GPU cluster -- because an iso-node comparison that hands one side a later interconnect is not iso anything, and this study previously gave the ROM array an NVLink-5 rate against an A100.

domain_size.note: Eight A100 SXM GPUs on one HGX/DGX A100 baseboard, connected by six second-generation NVSwitches. Past the eighth GPU every byte leaves the baseboard for the scale-out fabric, which is the second link class this study charges.
domain_size.source: https://www.nvidia.com/content/dam/en-zz/Solutions/Data-Center/HGX/pdf/nvidia-hgx-a100-datasheet.pdf ; NVIDIA DGX A100 System Architecture WP-10083-001_v01 (July 2020)

fabric.note: Single-tier all-to-all, stated verbatim: "Each A100 GPU uses twelve NVLink interconnects to communicate with all six NVSwitches, which means there are two links from each GPU to each switch." Every GPU pair is therefore one switch traversal apart and an in-domain collective has a rank-count-independent latency, which is also what the measured speed-of-light all-reduce floor shows.
fabric.source: NVIDIA DGX A100 System Architecture WP-10083-001_v01 (July 2020)

hop_latency_s.note: NVIDIA publishes no NVLink or NVSwitch latency figure in any form -- six first-party pages were checked and every one gives bandwidth only -- so this is assumed and swept. It is a per-traversal cost, and the collective model charges two traversals inside a domain, so the stated 1.5 us is a 3.0 us in-domain all-reduce. Measured comparators on GB200: a speed-of-light all-reduce floor of 1.404 us (0.306 us L2 round trip plus 0.792 us remote store), a best low-latency kernel at 2.37 us for a small message, and NCCL's ring at 11.0 us. The 1.0-5.5 us sweep therefore spans a 2.0-11.0 us all-reduce, which brackets the floor at one end and stock NCCL at the other; the STATED value sits near the optimistic end and so favours the GPU.
hop_latency_s.source: https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/data-center/nvlink/ ; Shen, Korzh, Bachan et al., Every us Matters: Achieving Near Speed-of-Light Latency in GPU Collectives, arXiv:2607.16100

bytes_s.note: 26.75 PB/s. Cerebras' own documents disagree on the unit -- the CS-3 cluster datasheet says 214 PB/s core-to-core and the WSE-2 weight-streaming paper says 220 Pb/s -- and 214 Pb/s is exactly 26.75 PB/s. This model takes the bit reading, which is eight times the more conservative of the two and is therefore the reading that does NOT flatter the wafer.

fabric.note: Stated verbatim: "The CS-1 wafer is an MIMD, distributed-memory machine with a 2D-mesh interconnection fabric... The routers link to the routers of the four neighboring tiles." There is no switch, so an all-reduce costs about 1.1 times the mesh diameter -- Cerebras measured their own at "a cycle count only about 10% greater than the diameter of the system" -- and not the flat two traversals a switched domain gets.
fabric.source: Rocki et al., Fast Stencil-Code Computation on a Wafer-Scale Processor, SC20, arXiv:2010.03660

hop_latency_s.note: 100 ns per on-wafer reticle-to-reticle hop; a stitched on-wafer link has no SerDes, no packet framing and no switch, so it is well under a package hop. Not measured, but it now has an independent cross-check: Cerebras publishes a single clock cycle per tile hop and roughly 900,000 cores over 46,225 mm2, which is about 73 tiles across one 815 mm2 reticle field, so a reticle crossing is on the order of 73 cycles. Swept 30-500 ns.
hop_latency_s.source: docs/WAFER_VERSUS_ARRAY_LATENCY.md ; Rocki et al., Fast Stencil-Code Computation on a Wafer-Scale Processor, SC20, arXiv:2010.03660

logic_density_vs_n7.note: N5 1.80x N7 multiplied by an assumed 1.10x N5->N4P logic-density step; the step itself is the assumed part

sram_hd_bitcell_um2.note: N4/N4P is an N5-family optical shrink; TSMC has not published an SRAM bitcell shrink over N5, so the N5 cell is carried over

logic_density_vs_n7.note: TSMC states N5 delivers ~1.8x the logic density of N7

sram_hd_bitcell_um2.note: TSMC ISSCC 2020: 0.021 um2 high-density 6T SRAM bitcell at N5

logic_density_vs_n7.note: TSMC: N6 delivers 18% higher logic density than N7

sram_hd_bitcell_um2.note: TSMC states N6 design rules are fully compatible with N7; the 6T HD bitcell is therefore carried over from N7 unchanged. The 18% N6 gain is a logic-standard-cell gain, not an SRAM bitcell gain.

logic_density_vs_n7.note: N7 is the density baseline for this table by definition

sram_hd_bitcell_um2.note: TSMC IEDM 2016 7nm platform, 0.027 um2 high-density 6T SRAM bitcell

purpose: Graded technology primitives for the area-constrained roofline model. Every entry is a primitive input; capacities, bandwidths and compute roofs are derived from these by src/opentallas/roofline.py and are never stated here.

hbm_stacks.note: five active HBM2e stacks on the 80GB part

die_area_mm2.note: two reticle-limited dies in one package, ~1600 mm2 of silicon per package

dies_per_package.note: counted per package for iso-area comparison

die_area_mm2.note: wafer-scale die, used only as the wafer area and fabric anchor

batch_size.note: The figure is quoted per user, so batch is modelled as 1 for the anchor. On this model's ROM weight path the anchor rate is batch-independent for a dense model, so the assumption does not move the anchor; it does move the aggregate throughput and the SRAM KV area.
batch_size.source: not published by Taalas; checked taalas.com, CNX Software, Wavect and Kaitchup

execution_format.note: canonical execution format 'w4a8'. Taalas publishes a custom 3-bit base type with a 3/6-bit mixture for weights; the activation width is not published and 8 bits is assumed. A model-specific ASIC freezes one datapath at manufacture, so the checkpoint's released BF16 arithmetic is NOT what this part executes and must not be priced at the BF16 roof.

output_tokens.note: 1K output sequence length; the quoted rate is sustained to a final context of 2048 tokens

power_w.note: reported around 250 W per PCIe card; a ten-card server is quoted at 2.5 kW

published_tokens_s_per_user.note: 16,960 tokens/s per user on Llama 3.1 8B at 1k input / 1k output. Every figure is self-run by Taalas; there is no MLPerf or third-party measurement, and the batch size is stated nowhere. The rounded '17k' on the product page is the same number.

weight_amortization.note: HC1 is a compute-in-ROM part: Bajic describes one transistor storing four bits and doing the multiply for them. Llama-3.1-8B is dense, so every token engages the whole array and per_stream and per_region are the same machine here. Evaluating the anchor as 'batched' would model a MAC array the part does not have, which matters now that the floorplan depends on the policy.
weight_amortization.source: Taalas publishes no batch size and no microarchitecture

weight_bits_per_parameter.note: Taalas publishes a custom 3-bit base type with a mixture of 3-bit and 6-bit parameters but no mix ratio. 3.5 bits/parameter is the stated point; sweep 3.0 to 6.0.

area_mm2.note: Taalas HC1 die area, used as the reticle-class chip area for array designs so the array and the anchor are the same unit of silicon

array_efficiency.note: Taken above the SRAM array efficiency because a ROM macro carries no write drivers and no write-assist circuitry. Sweep 0.60 to 0.80.
array_efficiency.source: no published mask-ROM macro floorplan at a leading node

cell_to_sram_cell_area_ratio.note: A contact/via-programmed NOR mask-ROM bit is one transistor with no write port, no write assist and no write redundancy, against a 6T SRAM bit. 1/6 to 1/4 brackets the plausible cell-area ratio; 1/5 is the stated point. This is the single most load-bearing assumption in the ROM capacity chain and must be swept.
cell_to_sram_cell_area_ratio.source: no fabricated leading-node mask-ROM bitcell has been published for this program

cim_cell_area_multiplier.note: area of a compute-in-ROM cell relative to a storage-only mask-ROM cell. A compute-in-ROM cell carries a pass transistor and the product-line wiring that lets it select one pre-computed partial product, on top of the via programming that stores its bits. Taalas describes one transistor per 4-bit parameter doing both, so the multiplier is small but cannot be 1.0. This is the second most load-bearing assumption in this file after the ROM-to-SRAM cell ratio, and it decides the storage-versus-compute-in-ROM comparison.
cim_cell_area_multiplier.source: no published compute-in-ROM bitcell at any node

cim_precompute_area_fraction.note: fraction of die area a compute-in-ROM part spends on the pre-computation block that forms every product of one activation with the small weight alphabet. At 3-bit weights that is 8 values, built from shifts and carry-save adders, and it replaces the dedicated MAC array entirely. Small by construction, which is the point of the architecture.
cim_precompute_area_fraction.source: derived shape only: 2^b shift-add units per activation-broadcast region

cross_checks.name: fabricated 28 nm hybrid SRAM/ROM-CIM macro density
cross_checks.note: 8.928 Mbit/mm2 at 28 nm on fabricated silicon. It is a compute-in-memory macro, so its density is a lower bound on a pure storage ROM array. Scaled to N6 by the same published bitcell-area ratio this model uses elsewhere (4.70x) it gives 42.0 Mbit/mm2 = 5.2 MB/mm2, against the 16.2 MB/mm2 this model derives for a storage-only array -- consistent with a CIM macro spending most of its area on compute. Cross-check only; not an input.

cross_checks.name: 3D-METRO transistorless 3D-metal ROM density
cross_checks.note: 20.7 MB/mm2 from a simulated evaluation, not fabricated silicon. Upper cross-check on the 16.2 MB/mm2 this model derives at N6 for a planar array. Cross-check only; not an input.

anchor_node_sram_hd_bitcell_um2.note: TSMC 28 nm HKMG high-density 6T SRAM bitcell, 0.127 um2. Used to scale the 28 nm ROM-CIM read-bandwidth density to the target node by published array-density ratio.

macro_area_mm2.note: simulated, not fabricated; carried over from configs/hardware/technology_inputs.json

operations_per_weight.note: one stored weight participates in one multiply-add per dense matrix-vector pass
operations_per_weight.source: definition, not a publication: one stored weight participates in one multiply and one add per dense matrix-vector pass, and the FLOP convention counts those as two operations. Regraded from `published` -- nobody published this, it is how the unit is defined, and calling a definition a publication is the same error class as calling a reading of an implementation a derivation.

read_bandwidth_scaling_rule.note: Read-bandwidth density is scaled by (anchor-node bitcell area / target-node bitcell area): the same macro throughput in proportionally less area. No clock-frequency bonus is applied on top. For 28 nm -> N6 this ratio is 4.70x, which corresponds to an effective density-scaling exponent of 1.005 on (28/6) -- the wire/periphery-limited CONSERVATIVE end of the 1.0-2.0 bracket documented in src/opentallas/technology.py. src/opentallas/technology.py documents 1.0-2.0 as the plausible exponent bracket; this rule sits at its conservative end.
read_bandwidth_scaling_rule.source: published 6T HD bitcell areas at 28 nm and at the target node

array_efficiency.note: bitcell area divided by total macro area including decoders, sense amplifiers, write drivers and redundancy. Published foundry macros land between 0.55 and 0.75; sweep that range.
array_efficiency.source: no vendor macro floorplan published for the target arrays

read_bandwidth_anchor.attribution_note: The derived density is charged against WHOLE-die area but is then applied only to the SRAM array area of a modelled design. WSE-2's SRAM occupies a minority of its die, so this is a conservative (low) bandwidth density for an SRAM array.

scaling_rule.note: as the ROM rule; the anchor is at N7 so the N7 and N6 ratios are 1.00
scaling_rule.source: published 6T HD bitcell areas at N7 and at the target node

cooling_limit_w_per_mm2.note: A100 SXM dissipates 400 W over an 826 mm2 die, 0.484 W/mm2, rounded to 0.50. Cross-checks: Taalas HC1 at a reported 250 W over 815 mm2 is 0.31 W/mm2, and a 15-23 kW wafer over 46,225 mm2 is 0.32-0.50 W/mm2.

units: areas mm^2 unless a field name says um2; bytes and bits decimal SI; times seconds; energy joules

reticle_regions.note: 46,225 mm2 divided by the 815 mm2 reticle field; sets the on-wafer pipeline hop count
